claims.text: High-temperature stability of near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles is maintained predominantly by kinetic limitations to elemental diffusion rather than by thermodynamic equilibrium.
The nanoparticles remain in a metastable, chemically homogeneous state during operational time scales.
Elemental diffusion is too slow during operation to permit segregation.
The initial materials are metastable, near-equiatomic, multielement solid-solution nanoparticles.
These nanoparticles can be synthesized through diverse physical or chemical routes.
The rate of elemental diffusion governs the onset or absence of measurable phase segregation.
High kinetic barriers prevent constituent elements from diffusing rapidly enough to reach a segregated state.
A segregated state is thermodynamically favored over the homogeneous high-entropy configuration under the relevant conditions.
The metastable high-entropy configuration persists until a critical combination of temperature and exposure time is exceeded.
Within expected operational time scales, the nanoparticles will exhibit minimal elemental segregation.
Within expected operational time scales, the nanoparticles will largely preserve a single-phase structure.
Increasing temperature or exposure time beyond the kinetic limit will eventually produce significant phase separation or segregation.
Room-temperature nanoparticles or nanoparticles subjected only to short-duration high-temperature exposure show no observable elemental rearrangement.
Above the kinetic threshold, phase separation may become rapid and governed by thermodynamic equilibrium.
The temperature-time threshold for breakdown of kinetic stabilization depends on elemental composition and fabrication history.
